subject: Maximum likelihood estimate of a discrete parameter vs sum over values

messages.author: cd58511bd9115a1c
messages.subject: Maximum likelihood estimate of a discrete parameter vs sum over values
parts:
I am interested in creating a model in which a two-state latent parameter underlying noisy data evolves over time as either random walk or is strictly zero. That is:

y[t] ~ normal(x[t], sigma_observation)

if state==1
    x[t] ~ normal(x[t-1], sigma_x)
if state==2
    x[t]=0

Ultimately it would be great to have a Markov transition probability scheme governing the state changes.

I've come up with two imperfect implementations for this model (not including state transition dynamics) and I was wondering which direction I should take, or if there was an alternative way of proceeding.

One implementation of this model is uses an indicator function such that:
             x[t] ~ normal(x[t-1], sigma_x);
             y[t] ~ normal(I[t]*x[t], sigma_observation);

where y is the noisy data which is a function of the latent variable x multiplied by an indicator function I, which can be 0 or 1 at each time.

Here is my implementation. The value of I at each time is determined by the maximum likelihood of y given I = 1 or I=0:

data {
    int<lower=1> N; // number of data points
    real y[N];// observations
}

parameters {
    real<lower=0> x[N];
    real sig2obs;
   
    real<lower=0> sigma;
}

model {
    real ll[2];
    int I[N];

    sigma ~ cauchy(0, 5);

    for (n in 1:N) {
        if (n==1){
            x[n] ~ normal(y[n], sig2obs);
        }else{
            x[n] ~ normal(x[n-1], sigma);
        }

        //Estimate likelihood with mu=0 or mu=x[n]      
        ll[1]=normal_lpdf(y[n] | 0, sig2obs);
        ll[2]=normal_lpdf(y[n] | x[n], sig2obs);
       
        //Set I based on the maximum likelihood
        if (ll[1]>ll[2]){
            I[n]=0;
        }else{
            I[n]=1;
        }

        y ~ normal(x[n]*I[n],sig2obs);
    }
}
 
This implementation appears to work, however, it is hard to check, as I can't get back the value for I since it is a local model variable. Is there a way to get back the indicator function or a variable that is equivalent to x[t]*I[t]?

The second implementation is based on the change point model in the manual, where we sum over possible values of x, which essentially makes x a mixture model of the random walk value and a mode around zero
data {
    int<lower=1> N;// number of data points
    real y[N];// observations  
}

parameters {
    real<lower=0> x[N];
    real sig2obs;
   
    real<lower=0> sigma;
    simplex[2] theta;
}

model {
    real ps[2];

    sigma ~ cauchy(0, 5);

    for (n in 1:N) {
        if(n==1){
            ps[1] = log(theta[1])+normal_lpdf(x[1] | 0, 1);
            ps[2] = log(theta[2])+normal_lpdf(x[1] | y[1], sigma);
        }else{
            ps[1] = log(theta[1]) + normal_lpdf(x[n] | 0, 1);
            ps[2] = log(theta[2]) + normal_lpdf(x[n] | x[n-1], sigma);
        }

        //Sum over zero and random walk states
        target += log_sum_exp(ps);
    }

    y ~ normal(x,sig2obs);
}

The main benefit of this implementation is that x itself shifts states and there is no need for an indicator function. It also sort of adds a bit of transition dynamics through the estimation of the mixture parameter theta. On the other hand, the value of of x is never strictly zero, which is what we would like to have. Also, it is unclear to me what the variance on the "zero" state should be.

Which way is best to proceed? Does either way lend itself better to developing transition probabilities between the states?

Thanks!

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Maximum likelihood estimate of a discrete parameter vs sum over values
parts:
The marginalization is the way to go. Stan's algorithms assume
the log density being implemented is continuously differentiable.
You can sometimes get the kind of thing you're doing in the first
example to work, but it converts Stan into something like a rejection
sampler, which tends not to be very efficient or even well tuned by
Stan's warmup procedures.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Maximum likelihood estimate of a discrete parameter vs sum over values
parts: Yes.

> On Nov 30, 2016, at 1:26 PM, ralphe...@gmail.com wrote:
>
> Thanks so much!
>
> Ultimately I would like to get the state at each time. Is there a way to get out the value of the local model variable?

No. You either have to save it as a transformed parameter
or redefine it in the generated quantities block (the latter
is cheap in run time but can be expensive in duplicated
code unless you use a user-defined function).
> I could implement the marginalization and use the same maximum likelihood scheme to tell which discrete state it was in at each time to report that post-hoc.
Exactly.
> Also, given a marginalization scheme, is it possible to implement a markov transition model between the states?

Yes, you can build HMMs. There are examples in the manual
and have been some interesting discussions online about
generalizations.

- Bob

messages.author: cd58511bd9115a1c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Maximum likelihood estimate of a discrete parameter vs sum over values
parts:
Thanks!

In a case like this with a latent variable, is it better to do the marginalization at the state or observation level. That is:

//Marginalize over the hidden state

ps[1] = log(theta[1]) + normal_lpdf(x[n] | 0, 1);
ps[2] = log(theta[2]) + normal_lpdf(x[n] | x[n-1], sigma);


//Sum over zero and random walk states
target += log_sum_exp(ps);

y[n] ~ normal(x[n],sig2obs);

VS
x[n] ~ normal(x[n-1], sigma);

ps[1] = log(theta[1]) + normal_lpdf(y[n] | 0, sigma_obs);
ps[2] = log(theta[2]) + normal_lpdf(y[n] | x[n], sigma_obs);

//Sum over zero and random walk states
target += log_sum_exp(ps);

What's nice about the second case is that you are truly allowing the state to be zero, at least in its effect on y.

Thanks!
